## What this notebook produces

For each selected species, a **weekly time series** of the share of that
species' total population that sits inside our study area (the Pacific
Flyway states). Plotted across the year, it shows migration through the
region as a pulse: the share rises as birds arrive and drops as they move on.

**Outputs** (both are *derived* products we're allowed to share):

- `data/derived/weekly_population_share.csv`: the numbers
- `figures/02_<season>_passage_curves.png`: the chart (season from config.R)

## Key ideas 

**Relative abundance is not a bird count.** eBird Status estimates the
expected count on a *standardized checklist*, not the number of birds on the
ground. So we can't say "2 million Wilson's Warblers are in California." What
we *can* say robustly is what **share of a species' population** is in a
place in a given week. That's what eBird's `proportion-population` product
gives us, and it's why we use it here instead of raw abundance.

**Never compare species' raw abundance values.** A value of 5 for one species
and 2 for another doesn't mean the first is 2.5× more common. Within-species
shares and timing are fine; cross-species magnitudes are not.

**The dates are a "typical year."** eBird models pool many years of
checklists. Layer dates such as `2023-09-20` mean "the week of Sep 20 in a
typical year," not September 2023 specifically.

```{r setup}
source(here::here("R", "config.R"))

library(ebirdst)
library(terra)    # rasters
library(sf)       # polygons
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

selection <- read_csv(file.path(PATHS$derived, "species_selection.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(selected)

selection |> select(species_code, common_name, use)
```

## Step 1 · Build the study area

We use the `maps` package's US state outlines because they ship with the
package (no download, no extra key) and are accurate enough at 27 km.
The building logic lives in `R/study_area.R` so notebooks 02 and 03 use
identical boundaries; read that file for the geometry details.

```{r study-area}
source(here::here("R", "study_area.R"))

states <- study_states()   # one polygon per state, CONUS Albers (EPSG:5070)

# One merged polygon for the whole flyway study area, plus the focus state.
study_area <- states |> summarise(name = "Pacific Flyway (study states)")
focus_area <- states |> filter(state == FOCUS_STATE) |>
  mutate(name = tools::toTitleCase(FOCUS_STATE)) |> select(name)

areas <- bind_rows(study_area, focus_area)

ggplot(states) + geom_sf() + labs(title = "Study area states") + theme_minimal()
```

## Step 2 · Download the eBird data (once per species)

```{r download}
# pattern = "_27km_" keeps only the 27 km files (see R/config.R for why).
# Files go to ebirdst_data_dir(), which is OUTSIDE this repo, so raw eBird
# rasters can never be committed to GitHub by accident.
# Already-downloaded files are skipped, so re-running this is cheap.
walk(selection$species_code, \(code) {
  ebirdst_download_status(
    code,
    download_abundance = TRUE,   # includes proportion-population
    pattern = paste0("_", EBIRD_RESOLUTION, "_")
  )
})
```

## Step 3 · Weekly share of each population inside the study area

```{r weekly-share}
#' Weekly share of a species' population inside each area.
#'
#' The proportion-population raster has 52 layers (one per week). In each
#' layer, every cell holds the fraction of the species' TOTAL population in
#' that cell, so the whole map sums to ~1. Summing the cells that fall
#' inside a polygon gives the fraction of the population inside it.
weekly_share <- function(code) {
  prop <- load_raster(code,
                      product = "proportion-population",
                      period = "weekly",
                      resolution = EBIRD_RESOLUTION)

  # eBird rasters use their own equal-area projection. Reproject OUR
  # polygons to match the raster (much faster and more exact than
  # reprojecting a 52-layer raster to match the polygons).
  areas_proj <- st_transform(areas, crs(prop))

  # extract(..., fun = sum) adds up every cell whose CENTER falls inside
  # each polygon, separately for each of the 52 weekly layers.
  # Result: one row per area, one column per week.
  sums <- terra::extract(prop, vect(areas_proj), fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE,
                         ID = FALSE)

  # Layer names are the week dates ("2023-01-04", ...). Re-apply them
  # explicitly so they can't get mangled into "X2023.01.04" on the way
  # through data.frame().
  names(sums) <- names(prop)

  sums |>
    mutate(area = areas$name) |>
    pivot_longer(-area, names_to = "week_date", values_to = "share") |>
    mutate(species_code = code,
           week_date = as.Date(week_date))
}

shares <- map_dfr(selection$species_code, weekly_share) |>
  left_join(selection |> select(species_code, common_name,
                                season_start, season_end),
            by = "species_code") |>
  mutate(
    # Flag weeks inside each species' own eBird migration season (the one set
    # in config.R). Season dates are species-specific (hummingbirds move
    # earlier than most warblers), so we don't use one fixed date range.
    in_season = week_date >= as.Date(season_start) & week_date <= as.Date(season_end)
  )

write_csv(shares, file.path(PATHS$derived, "weekly_population_share.csv"))
```

## Step 4 · Summary table for the report

```{r summary}
season_summary <- shares |>
  filter(in_season) |>
  group_by(common_name, area) |>
  summarise(
    peak_week  = week_date[which.max(share)],
    peak_share = max(share),     # max fraction of population in the area
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(peak_week = format(peak_week, "%b %d"),   # drop the nominal year
         peak_share = scales::percent(peak_share, accuracy = 0.1))

season_summary
```

## Step 5 · Passage curves

```{r plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
p <- shares |>
  filter(area == study_area$name) |>
  ggplot(aes(week_date, share)) +
  # Shade each species' migration season so the pulse is easy to see.
  geom_rect(
    data = \(d) distinct(d, common_name, season_start, season_end),
    aes(xmin = as.Date(season_start), xmax = as.Date(season_end),
        ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ common_name, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b", date_breaks = "2 months") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of each population inside the Pacific Flyway study states",
    subtitle = paste0("Weekly, typical year. Grey band = eBird's ", SEASON_LABEL,
                      " migration season for that species."),
    x = NULL, y = "Share of population",
    caption = FIGURE_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p
ggsave(file.path(PATHS$figures, paste0("02_", SEASON_LABEL, "_passage_curves.png")),
       p, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 200)
```

## How to read the curves

- A species that **breeds** in the study states climbs during spring
  migration and stays high through summer.
- A species that **passes through** (winters farther south, breeds farther
  north) shows a **hump** in its migration season: a rise, then a drop.
- Comparing the spring and fall humps for the same species is evidence for
  **looped migration** (different routes each way): a higher spring hump means
  more of the population routes through our states going north.
- The **peak week** in the summary table is our estimate of peak passage.
  Notebook 04 compares those weeks with radar-measured nightly volumes over
  Southern California.
